meta.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma
meta.note: Seed dataset: Dhyānam + Namas 1–26 (Shlokas 1–10). Use `npm run data:merge` to add the rest.

shlokas.label: Dhyānam 1
shlokas.devanagari:
सिन्दूरारुणविग्रहां त्रिनयनां माणिक्यमौलिस्फुरत्
तारानायकशेखरां स्मितमुखीमापीनवक्षोरुहाम् ।
पाणिभ्यामलिपूर्णरत्नचषकं रक्तोत्पलं बिभ्रतीं
सौम्यां रत्नघटस्थरक्तचरणां ध्यायेत्परामम्बिकाम् ॥
shlokas.iast:
sindūrāruṇavigrahāṃ trinayanāṃ māṇikyamaulisphurat
tārānāyakaśekharāṃ smitamukhīmāpīnavakṣoruhām |
pāṇibhyāmalipūrṇaratnacaṣakaṃ raktotpalaṃ bibhratīṃ
saumyāṃ ratnaghaṭastharaktacaraṇāṃ dhyāyetparāmambikām ||
shlokas.englishTranslation: Let one meditate on the Supreme Mother: her body red as vermilion, three-eyed, her ruby-studded crown crested with the crescent moon, her face softly smiling, her bosom full. In her hands she bears a jewelled cup brimming with nectar and a red lotus; gentle in aspect, her red feet rest upon a jewelled pot.

shlokas.label: Dhyānam 2
shlokas.devanagari:
अरुणां करुणातरङ्गिताक्षीं
धृतपाशाङ्कुशपुष्पबाणचापाम् ।
अणिमादिभिरावृतां मयूखैर्
अहमित्येव विभावये भवानीम् ॥
shlokas.iast:
aruṇāṃ karuṇātaraṅgitākṣīṃ
dhṛtapāśāṅkuśapuṣpabāṇacāpām |
aṇimādibhirāvṛtāṃ mayūkhair
ahamityeva vibhāvaye bhavānīm ||
shlokas.englishTranslation: I contemplate Bhavānī, the dawn-red Mother, her eyes rippling with compassion, holding the noose, the goad, the flower-arrows and the bow, encircled by the rays of Aṇimā and the other siddhis — contemplating her as “I am She.”

shlokas.label: Dhyānam 3
shlokas.devanagari:
ध्यायेत्पद्मासनस्थां विकसितवदनां पद्मपत्रायताक्षीं
हेमाभां पीतवस्त्रां करकलितलसद्धेमपद्मां वराङ्गीम् ।
सर्वालङ्कारयुक्तां सततमभयदां भक्तनम्रां भवानीं
श्रीविद्यां शान्तमूर्तिं सकलसुरनुतां सर्वसम्पत्प्रदात्रीम् ॥
shlokas.iast:
dhyāyetpadmāsanasthāṃ vikasitavadanāṃ padmapatrāyatākṣīṃ
hemābhāṃ pītavastrāṃ karakalitalasaddhemapadmāṃ varāṅgīm |
sarvālaṅkārayuktāṃ satatamabhayadāṃ bhaktanamrāṃ bhavānīṃ
śrīvidyāṃ śāntamūrtiṃ sakalasuranutāṃ sarvasampatpradātrīm ||
shlokas.englishTranslation: Let one meditate on Bhavānī — Śrīvidyā — seated on a lotus, her face in full bloom, her eyes long as lotus petals, golden-hued and robed in yellow, a shining golden lotus in her hand; fair of limb, adorned with every ornament, ever bestowing fearlessness, gracious to those who bow to her, serene in form, praised by all the gods, giver of every prosperity.
The auspicious Mother; the great Empress; Sovereign of the splendid lion-throne; born from the fire-pit of pure consciousness; intent on accomplishing the work of the gods.
Radiant as a thousand rising suns; endowed with four arms; rich with the noose that is desire; shining with the goad that is wrath.
Her bow of sugarcane is the mind; her arrows are the five subtle elements; the flood of her own red radiance bathes the entire sphere of the cosmos.
Her hair gleams with campaka, aśoka, punnāga and saugandhika blossoms; she is adorned with a crown ablaze with rows of ruby-gems.
Her forehead shines like the half-moon of the eighth lunar day; the musk-mark upon it is like the dark spot on the moon of her face.
Her brows are festive archways at the gate of the auspicious house of Kāma that is her face; her eyes are like fish darting in the overflowing stream of her facial beauty.
Graced with a nose like a fresh campaka bud; shining with a nose-jewel that outshines the stars.
Captivating with ear-ornaments of kadamba blossom-clusters; the discs of the sun and moon serve as her twin ear-rings.
Her cheeks surpass a mirror of ruby; her lips put to shame the beauty of fresh coral and of the bimba fruit.
Brilliant with two rows of teeth like the sprouts of Śuddhavidyā; the fragrance of her camphor-scented betel draws in every quarter of space.

sections.title: Phala Śruti
sections.description: Concluding verses on the fruits of recitation

namas.meaning: The Auspicious Mother
namas.commentary: The stotra opens with motherhood itself. In the traditional reading the first three names trace the three cosmic functions — śrīmātā for creation (Srishti), śrīmahārājñī for sustenance (Sthiti), and śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī for dissolution (Saṃhāra). “Mātā” is also read as “she who measures out (mā) the universe”, the power by which the formless Brahman takes measure and name.

namas.meaning: The Great Empress
namas.commentary: Having created as Mother, she now rules as sovereign — the sustaining, governing aspect (Sthiti). Her empire is the whole manifest cosmos, and her rule is not conquest but the natural order held in place by her will. The adjective “great” marks her as sovereign even over the sovereigns, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra among them.

namas.meaning: Sovereign of the splendid lion-throne
namas.commentary: She is enthroned on the Siṃhāsana. The tradition reads the throne esoterically — its supports are the great deities and its seat the Sadāśiva-tattva — so that the seat of power is itself the whole creative-dissolving apparatus. Completing the triad, the one who sits above all is the one into whom all finally withdraws (Saṃhāra).

namas.meaning: Born from the fire-pit of pure consciousness
namas.commentary: Outwardly this recalls the Purāṇic account of the gods' great sacrifice from whose fire she appeared. Inwardly, the fire-pit is Cit itself and the sacrifice is the offering of the whole world into awareness; she is not produced by an act but is the self-luminous flame of consciousness. Practitioners also relate the “pit” to the Kuṇḍalinī locus, where the same fire is kindled in sādhana.

namas.meaning: Ever intent on accomplishing the work of the gods
namas.commentary: Her appearance has a purpose: to restore the gods' rightful order (in the narrative, by destroying Bhaṇḍāsura). Read inwardly, the “gods” are the presiding powers of the senses and faculties, and “their work” is the liberation of the individual; she is always poised to act for it. The name thus ends the first verse by tying her majesty to compassion.

namas.meaning: Radiant as a thousand rising suns
namas.commentary: The description of her form begins with light. The sun at dawn is red rather than harsh, so the simile conveys both overwhelming brilliance and a gentle, motherly red (aruṇa), the colour the dhyāna verses insist upon.

namas.meaning: Endowed with four arms
namas.commentary: Her four arms hold the noose, goad, bow and arrows (named in the next two verses). Traditionally the four arms are also read as the four Vedas, the four goals of life (puruṣārthas), or the four inner faculties — mind, intellect, ego and memory — each held in her service.

namas.meaning: Rich with the noose that is desire
namas.commentary: The noose in her upper left hand is Rāga: the pull of love and desire by which she binds the world to itself and draws the devotee toward her. The same power that binds ordinary beings becomes, once turned toward the Mother, the cord that draws the seeker home.

namas.meaning: Shining with the goad that is wrath
namas.commentary: The goad in her upper right hand is Krodha — not personal rage but the force that checks and corrects, as a mahout's hook restrains an elephant. The noose draws; the goad restrains: together they are her twofold means of governing the mind.

namas.meaning: Whose sugarcane bow is the mind
namas.commentary: Her bow is sweet sugarcane — the mind, whose nature is sweet yet pliant and which is drawn taut between sankalpa and vikalpa. By holding the mind as her bow she reveals that the faculty which scatters the unliberated is, in her hand, an instrument of grace.

namas.meaning: Whose arrows are the five subtle elements

wordBreakdown.meaning: subtle element (sound, touch, form, taste, smell)

namas.commentary: Her five flower-arrows are the five tanmātras — śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa and gandha — the subtle essences from which the senses and the gross elements arise. They are the “flowers” with which she pierces the heart of the world; the whole sensory universe is her gentle weaponry.

namas.meaning: Whose own red radiance floods and bathes the whole sphere of the cosmos
namas.commentary: The red glow that began as the ornament of her body now overflows and fills the Brahmāṇḍa. The universe is not outside her light but immersed in it, as a lotus is bathed in dawn. The first stage of the physical portrait closes by expanding from her person to the whole world.

namas.meaning: Whose hair gleams with campaka, aśoka, punnāga and saugandhika blossoms
namas.commentary: From this verse the description proceeds from the crown downward, the traditional order for dhyāna on a form (keśādi-pādānta). Each flower is named for its fragrance and colour, making the Mother's hair a garden. The sequence also teaches the method of visualisation: part by part, from head to foot.

namas.meaning: Adorned with a crown blazing with rows of ruby-gems
namas.commentary: The crown (koṭīra) crowns the hair of the previous name. Its red gems echo her complexion, so the whole figure is chromatically unified in red and gold — the visual signature of Lalitā, in contrast to the white of Sarasvatī or the dark of Kālī.

namas.meaning: Whose forehead shines like the half-moon of the eighth lunar day

wordBreakdown.meaning: the moon of the eighth tithi (half-moon)

namas.commentary: Her forehead is a crescent-bounded half-moon, neither waxing nor waning in excess. Tradition hears in this a reference to the Ājñā region, where the inner moon is contemplated, and to the balance of the two halves of the lunar fortnight held in perfect symmetry.

namas.meaning: Whose musk-mark is like the dark spot on the moon of her face
namas.commentary: The tilaka of musk is likened to the lunar “stain” — yet here the spot is not a flaw but the one touch of darkness that sets off the brilliance of the face. The poetic conceit allows a quiet theological hint: even a mark of limitation, in her, becomes ornament.

namas.meaning: Whose brows are festive archways at the gateway of the auspicious house of Kāma that is her face
namas.commentary: Her face is likened to the auspicious dwelling of Kāma, and her curved eyebrows to the garlanded arches hung over its door at a festival. The image invites entry: the beauty of the face is the gateway through which the mind is drawn inward.

namas.meaning: Whose eyes are like fish darting in the overflowing stream of her facial beauty
namas.commentary: Her eyes dart like fish (mīna) in the channel of beauty overflowing from her face. Fish are said to sleep with open eyes and to nurture their young by sight alone — which is why the tradition calls her gaze, like the fish's, a source of grace (dṛk-dīkṣā) for devotees.

namas.meaning: Graced with a nose like a fresh campaka bud
namas.commentary: The straight, delicate ridge of the nose is compared to an unopened campaka bud. The comparison also carries a point of lore: bees are said never to alight on the campaka, so it is the image of a beauty that attracts without being tasted — an apt figure for the Mother who is approached by devotion, not possessed.

namas.meaning: Shining with a nose-jewel that outshines the stars
namas.commentary: Her nose-jewel eclipses the stars. Commentators note that “tārā” can also refer to the bright planet Venus and to the pearl, so the verse yields a layered image of a single point of white brilliance against the red of her complexion.

namas.meaning: Captivating with ear-ornaments fashioned from kadamba blossom-clusters
namas.commentary: The kadamba is dear to the Mother — the Kadamba forest is one of her chief abodes in the Purāṇic geography of Śrīpura. Wearing its blossoms at her ears marks her closeness to that sacred grove and anticipates the many names that refer to the Kadamba-vana.

namas.meaning: The discs of the sun and moon serve as her twin ear-rings
namas.commentary: Sun and moon, the two great luminaries, are her ear-rings: time itself (day and night, Sūrya and Candra) is an ornament that she wears. Esoterically they are the two nāḍīs, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, which flank the central channel along which the Kuṇḍalinī rises.

namas.meaning: Whose cheeks surpass a mirror of ruby
namas.commentary: A mirror cut from ruby would be both red and reflective; her cheek is more lustrous still. The name ends in -bhūḥ (a long-ū stem), so its mantra form takes the dative -bhuve (Padmarāga…kapolabhuve) rather than the usual -āyai — worth noting for correct recitation.

namas.meaning: Whose lips put to shame the beauty of fresh coral and the bimba fruit
namas.commentary: Coral and the red bimba fruit are the standard comparisons for red lips; here both are put to shame. Because the lips are the seat of speech, the tradition also hears in this the red radiance of Vāk, the Mother as the source of all utterance.

namas.meaning: Brilliant with two rows of teeth like the sprouts of Śuddhavidyā
namas.commentary: “Dvija” — twice-born — is a word for teeth, which are born twice. Her teeth are compared to the first sprouts of Śuddhavidyā, the pure knowledge in which Śrīvidyā culminates. Her smile is thus a seed-form of the same knowledge by which the aspirant is liberated.

namas.meaning: The fragrance of whose camphor-scented betel draws in every quarter of space
namas.commentary: Chewing the camphor-scented betel is the royal pleasure of an empress, and its fragrance fills the ten directions. The scent that draws all beings in is read as her grace (anugraha), which, like fragrance, reaches those who do not yet know its source.
